newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia begins building space craft for Alpha.
newsitem.headline: Russia begins building space craft for Alpha.

text.p: A Russian rocket company has started making the spacecraft that will bring a U.S.-Russian crew to the new Alpha international space station in 1999, a senior company official said on Tuesday.
The expected announcement was good news for the Russian space programme, which has suffered financial setbacks in recent months that have prompted delays in its contributions to Alpha.
"We will produce the craft according to schedule," said the official, who asked not to be named. "Usually we need about two years to build such a spacecraft."

His company, the state-owned Energiya Space Rocket Corporation based outside Moscow, has extensive experience building spacecraft that have journeyed to the orbiting Mir station over the past 11 years.
The official said the total production cost of the Soyuz craft, pre-launch tests, launch and control flight until docking with the orbiting station will be $50 million.
About 75 plants in Russia and the Commonwealth Independent States would supply spare parts, equipment and systems for the Soyuz, the official said in an interview.
Energiya has produced 25 Soyuz craft and 50 Progress cargo ships which were launched to the Russian Mir station, the only research centre orbiting Earth.
Unlike the U.S. shuttle, the Russian rocket propelling the craft at liftoff must be replaced every time, as only the top capsule remains after blast-off.

Another Russian rocket manufacturer, the Khrunichev space centre, said last week it had finished ground tests on the first module of the Alpha and planned to ship it to the Baikonur cosmodrome in Kazakhstan in December.
The module will be launched in June 1998, following Moscow's postponement from the original schedule of November this year.

The delay, caused by Russia's financial problems, provoked protests from the United States and other Western participants who warned that the entire Alpha project, to be built in stages by 2003, might be in jeopardy.

Khrunichev senior programme manager Sergei Shayevich recently said that a heavy booster Proton which will take the first Alpha module to a 220-km (137-mile) orbit was being assembled on schedule. "It will be delivered to Baikonur in August," he said.

Last month, the Russian Space Agency said Russia's work on 12 of Alpha's total of 36 modules would cost $3.2 billion. The United States plans to build 18 modules worth $17.2 billion. The European Space Agency, Japan, Canada and Italy are also contributing.

Khrunichev is now funding the construction of the second accommodation module, where the cosmonauts will live and work. In April, the Russian government promised 1.5 trillion roubles ($261 million) to fund the construction and the centre hoped to get the money soon.
